introduction-escaping-the-cli-limitation.core: kubectl is powerful but verbose: navigating relationships, watching many resources and switching contexts takes many commands. UIs and power tools (Kubernetes Dashboard, Lens/Freelens, k9s, Headlamp, Octant historically) and kubectl plugins via Krew speed up exploration and troubleshooting, without replacing GitOps for changes.

first_principles.problem: Engineers type 20 kubectl commands to follow one failing Pod from Deployment to logs and events.
truths: Visual and interactive views speed navigation.
Changes should still go through Git.

analogy.title: A file manager versus typing ls and cd for everything
analogy.breaks: File managers can edit freely; cluster changes from UIs bypass review unless restricted.

example.title: Following a failure
flow: l for logs, d for describe

check.q: Why should cluster UIs be used mostly read-only?
check.a: Changes made through UIs bypass code review and drift from the Git source of truth.

the-official-kubernetes-dashboard.core: Kubernetes Dashboard is the official web UI for viewing and managing resources, logs and exec. It runs in-cluster and authenticates with bearer tokens or a proxy. Historically, exposed dashboards with over-privileged service accounts caused major breaches (Tesla's cryptojacking), so expose it only internally with least privilege.

first_principles.problem: A public Dashboard bound to cluster-admin lets attackers deploy crypto miners.
truths: Service account permissions define what the UI can do.
derivation: Access via **kubectl proxy/port-forward** or SSO proxy.
Use **user tokens**, not a shared admin SA.

analogy.title: A building's control room
analogy.story: Useful for staff, catastrophic if left unlocked to the street.
analogy.breaks: Control rooms have guards; dashboards rely entirely on your auth configuration.

example.title: Safe access

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Local-only access with personal, limited permissions.

code.text:
kubectl -n kubernetes-dashboard port-forward svc/kubernetes-dashboard-kong-proxy 8443:443
# log in with your own short-lived token
kubectl create token alice-viewer -n kubernetes-dashboard

example.outcome: useful UI without a breach risk.

check.q: What famous risk is associated with the Kubernetes Dashboard?
check.a: Publicly exposed dashboards with admin privileges being used by attackers (e.g. for crypto-mining).

lens-the-kubernetes-ide.core: Lens (and its open-source fork Freelens) is a desktop Kubernetes IDE: it reads kubeconfigs, shows clusters, workloads and relationships visually, provides logs, terminals, port-forwarding, metrics charts (with Prometheus) and Helm management. It's local, uses your credentials and is good for exploration across many clusters.

first_principles.problem: Developers juggling five clusters lose track of contexts and namespaces.

analogy.title: An IDE for clusters
analogy.story: Like a code editor with file tree, terminal and debugger in one window.
analogy.breaks: IDEs edit local files; Lens acts on live clusters, so mistakes are immediate.

example.title: Investigating memory
flow: Open Pod → metrics chart shows leak

check.q: How does Lens authenticate to clusters?
check.a: Using your existing kubeconfig contexts and credentials.

k9s-the-terminal-power-users-tool.core: k9s is a fast terminal UI over the Kubernetes API: navigate resources with vim-like commands (:pods, :deploy), filter (/), view logs (l), describe (d), shell (s), port-forward (shift-f), delete or scale, switch contexts and namespaces, and use plugins, skins and XRay views of relationships. It's ideal over SSH and for keyboard-driven operators.

first_principles.problem: On-call engineers waste minutes typing kubectl commands during incidents.

analogy.title: A cockpit with shortcuts on every button
analogy.story: Experienced pilots fly by muscle memory.
analogy.breaks: Cockpits have safety covers on dangerous switches; enable k9s read-only mode for similar protection.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Diagnosis in seconds, no accidental changes.

check.q: How do you start k9s in a mode that prevents modifications?

octant-visualizing-relationships.core: Octant was a VMware developer-focused web UI that visualised resource relationships (Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pods → Services), with a plugin system. It's archived, but its idea of graph views lives on in Headlamp, Lens maps, k9s XRay and tools like kubectl tree and kube-lineage.

first_principles.problem: Developers can't see which Service, ConfigMap and Secret a failing Pod depends on.
truths: Objects relate via owners and selectors.
Tools come and go; concepts remain.

analogy.title: A family tree for resources
analogy.story: See who created whom and who depends on whom.
analogy.breaks: Family trees are fixed; resource graphs change with every rollout.

code.text:
kubectl krew install tree
kubectl tree deployment api -n shop
# Deployment/api → ReplicaSet/api-7f9 → Pod/api-7f9-abc ...

check.q: What kubectl plugin shows a resource's ownership hierarchy?

krew-the-plugin-manager.core: Krew is a package manager for kubectl plugins: install, update and discover hundreds of plugins (ctx/ns for context switching, tree, neat, who-can, sniff, view-secret, resource-capacity, stern for multi-Pod logs). Any executable named kubectl-<name> on PATH becomes a kubectl subcommand.

first_principles.problem: Each engineer has a different set of hand-installed scripts for common tasks.
truths: kubectl supports plugins by naming convention.
A package manager keeps tools consistent.
derivation: Install core plugins (**ctx, ns, tree, neat, who-can**).
**Review** plugins before use (they run locally with your creds).

analogy.title: An app store for your multitool
analogy.story: Add new blades to the same handle.
analogy.breaks: Multitools are physical; plugins are code with access to your clusters.

code.text:
kubectl krew install ctx ns tree neat who-can resource-capacity
kubectl ctx prod-eu && kubectl ns shop
kubectl who-can delete pods -n shop
kubectl resource-capacity --util

check.a: Any executable named kubectl-<name> on the PATH becomes 'kubectl <name>'.
